pages.t: A promise to a dying wife
pages.x: In 1631 Mumtaz Mahal, wife of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, died giving birth to their fourteenth child while travelling with him on campaign. Legend says she asked him, as she lay dying, to build her a tomb the world had never seen.

Shah Jahan chose a garden by the Yamuna river at Agra. Work began in 1632 under the architect Ustad Ahmad Lahori, and some 20,000 workers came from across the empire and beyond: stonecutters, inlayers, calligraphers and masons.
White marble came from Makrana, some 400 km away, hauled by more than a thousand elephants and teams of oxen.
pages.fx: The tomb with its great dome and four minarets took about 12 years. The gardens, mosque and gates were finished around 1653.

pages.x: The marble is inlaid with flowers made of as many as 28 kinds of precious and semi-precious stones, and with verses of the Quran in black marble letters that grow larger toward the top, so that from below they all look the same size.

The four minarets lean very slightly outwards, so that in an earthquake they would fall away from the tomb. Everything is laid out in perfect symmetry, except Shah Jahan's own coffin, squeezed in later beside his wife's.
In 1658 Shah Jahan's son Aurangzeb seized the throne and locked his father in the fort at Agra. For his last eight years, the story goes, the old emperor gazed across the river at his wife's tomb.

A legend says Shah Jahan meant to build a second tomb for himself across the river, in black marble, joined to the first by a bridge. Historians find no sign of it. But the garden on the far bank was laid out for viewing the Taj by moonlight.

The Taj Mahal is often called the most beautiful building in the world, a symbol of India and of love. Millions visit it every year, and India works hard to keep its marble white against the pollution of a modern city.
pts: Some 20,000 workers and a thousand elephants
